summary: No orders: markets are closed today for Thanksgiving, the S&P 500 fund ended Wednesday about 2% below its 200-day average after a hot inflation figure, so the buy-back signal has not come; the cash waits for that signal or 10 December at the latest, and the health care fund stays because it is well above its sell line.
thesis:
Where the account stands. At the end of Wednesday 25 November it was worth $971.90 against $943.26 for the benchmark, $1,000 left in an S&P 500 fund, a lead of about $29. Eleven trading days is still far too short to call this skill or luck.

Timing. US stock markets are closed today, Thursday 26 November, for Thanksgiving, and close early, at 1 p.m. New York time, on Friday. Any order written today would fill at Friday's open.

What has happened since the last decision:

- Wednesday opened with a deep fall and then recovered most of it. The S&P 500 ended down 0.25%, the Nasdaq Composite down 0.6% and the Dow up 0.3%, after being more than 1,100 points lower during the morning. The Nasdaq 100 fund QQQ was down more than 4% before noon and ended down 0.65%. Nvidia fell another 3.9%. The market's fear gauge, the VIX, ended near 28, still high.
- October PCE inflation, the Fed's preferred measure, rose 3.8% over the year, in line with forecasts, but the core measure, which leaves out food and energy, rose 3.3%, above what economists expected. Growth for the third quarter was revised up to a 4.3% yearly pace, and new claims for unemployment benefits were low at 189,000. Together these make a rate increase at the Fed meeting on 9 December look more certain.
- The US trade office proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 economies, from 15% for the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan up to 35% for Vietnam. These are proposals; comments are due on 5 January 2027, so nothing takes effect soon.
- The 10-year Treasury yield eased to about 4.85%.

Each holding judged against what I wrote when I bought it:

1. XLV: keep. It ended Wednesday at $183.68, down 0.6% on the day, about 4% above the $176 sell line and above its 50-day average ($177.39). I found no report widening the Medicare proposal that was named as the other reason to sell. Company news in health care on Wednesday (a delay to an FDA decision for Vertex, a production pause at Pharming) was specific to those companies, not the sector. It is about 3.5% below what I paid. It has done its job of holding up while the market falls. If it ends any day below $176, the next decision sells it.

2. Cash, about $827 (85%). The plan buys back the S&P 500 fund SPY when it ends two trading days in a row at least 1% above its 200-day average. That average is $733.16, so the line is about $740.49. SPY ended Wednesday at $716.70, about 2.2% below the average and about 3.2% below the line. With today closed, the earliest the signal could come is the end of Monday 30 November, and only if SPY ends both Friday's short session and Monday above $740.49. Buying at Friday's open would be acting before the signal on the thinnest trading day of the year. So I wait. The written end date stands: the account goes back to being fully invested no later than 10 December, the first trading day after the Fed decision, whether or not the signal comes.

I looked again at other uses for the cash. Consumer staples (XLP) is above all its averages and up 6.3% in 20 days, but a stay of about nine trading days would cost about 0.3% in fees with no specific, checkable reason beyond momentum. Treasury bills (SGOV) would earn less than the fees over that time. Longer bond funds (IEF, TLT) have risen as yields fell, but the core inflation surprise makes a further fall in yields less certain. Chip and technology funds remain far below their averages. None meets the plan's bar today.

This is not the first decision of the month, so there is no monthly review. The first is due at the start of December.
risks: If the market climbs strongly through Friday and next week, the account will give back its lead and may buy back above the price at which SPY was sold. If the market keeps falling, the 10 December date could put the cash back in at a bad moment. A larger-than-expected Fed increase on 9 December, or tariff news, could hit stocks and push XLV toward its $176 line. Friday's short session has little trading, so its prices can move more than usual. Figures differ somewhat between sources taken at different times.
